speaker: Unknown
en: Hello, and welcome back to The Cognitive Revolution.
zh: 大家好,欢迎回到 The Cognitive Revolution。

speaker: Unknown
en: Today, my guest is Eric Bigelow, member of technical staff at unicorn mechanistic interpretability startup, Goodfire.
zh: 今天我的嘉宾是 Eric Bigelow,独角兽机制可解释性初创公司 Goodfire 的技术成员。

speaker: Unknown
en: The story behind this episode is unique.
zh: 这期节目背后的故事很独特。

speaker: Unknown
en: After recently speaking with Bronson Shane of Apollo Research, who explained that even with access to models internal chain of thought, it is still often extremely difficult to determine how a model will decide to act, I asked Claude to survey the literature to see what the field as a whole understands about how these critical decision tokens are chosen.
zh: 在最近与 Apollo Research 的 Bronson Shane 交谈后——他解释说,即使能访问模型的内部思维链,要确定模型会如何决定行动,往往仍然极其困难——我让 Claude 调研了相关文献,想看看整个领域对这些关键决策 token 是如何被选中的到底了解多少。

speaker: Unknown
en: One name kept coming up in that thread and it was Eric.
zh: 在那条线程里,有一个名字不断出现,那就是 Eric。

speaker: Unknown
en: Eric recently completed a PhD in the Harvard psychology department with a dissertation titled, Toward a Cognitive Science of Large Language Models.
zh: Eric 最近在哈佛心理学系完成了博士学位,博士论文题目是《迈向大型语言模型的认知科学》。

speaker: Unknown
en: And while some of his academic colleagues initially questioned his pivot to focus on LLMs, the fact that even elite academic institutions are now willing to engage with AIs as a sort of mind strikes me as very notable indeed.
zh: 虽然他的一些学术同事最初质疑他转向专注 LLM,但如今连顶尖学术机构都愿意把 AI 当作某种心智来对待,这一点在我看来确实非常值得注意。

speaker: Unknown
en: We start today with a survey of Eric's work over the last couple of years, beginning with his 2024 paper on Forking Paths in Neural Text Generation, in which he conducted a massive resampling experiment at every token of a model's chain of thought to identify the critical tokens where uncertainty around the final answer suddenly collapses.
zh: 我们今天从回顾 Eric 过去几年的工作开始,先从他那篇 2024 年关于神经文本生成中分叉路径(Forking Paths)的论文讲起,在论文中他进行了一场大规模重采样实验,在模型思维链的每一个 token 上都重新采样,以识别出围绕最终答案的不确定性突然坍缩的那些关键 token。

speaker: Unknown
en: As so often with LLMs, some of the findings were intuitive, while others were quite surprising and at times difficult to interpret.
zh: 和 LLM 领域常见的情况一样,有些发现是符合直觉的,而另一些则相当出人意料,有时还很难解读。

speaker: Unknown
en: Interestingly, Eric says that a system's decisions are actually taken not so much by the model itself, but by the process of sampling from the model's final token distribution.
zh: 有意思的是,Eric 说系统的决策实际上并不是由模型本身做出的,而是由从模型最终 token 分布中采样的过程做出的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Which means that while the stochastic parrot paradigm should definitely be retired, stochasticity still plays an important role in model behavior.
zh: 这意味着,虽然「随机鹦鹉」范式确实应该被抛弃了,但随机性在模型行为中仍然扮演着重要角色。

speaker: Unknown
en: Eric frames much of what we are seeking to understand about LLMs in terms of in-context learning, emphasizing that few-shot prompts are just one clear example of how much runtime context can shape model behavior.
zh: Eric 把我们试图理解的关于 LLM 的许多内容都用上下文学习(in-context learning)来框定,他强调,少样本提示只是运行时上下文能在多大程度上塑造模型行为的一个清晰例子。

speaker: Unknown
en: His bet is that this flexibility means that improved harnesses and memory systems will out-compete per user fine-tuning, and thus that our focus of study should remain on major foundation models.
zh: 他的判断是,这种灵活性意味着改进的 harness 和记忆系统将会在与按用户微调的竞争中胜出,因此我们的研究重点应该继续放在主要的基础模型上。

speaker: Unknown
en: Along the way, we also discuss why 7 to 8 billion parameters currently seems to be the interpretability sweet spot, why KimiK3 was a step function for studying frontier-level coding and reward hacking, and why, for now at least, interpretability outside of the frontier model companies does meaningfully depend on Chinese open-weights models.
zh: 一路上,我们还讨论了为什么 70 到 80 亿参数目前似乎可解释性的最佳甜蜜点,为什么 KimiK3 是研究前沿级编程和奖励黑客(reward hacking)的一个阶跃函数,以及为什么至少在目前,前沿模型公司之外的可解释性确实在很大程度上依赖中国的开源权重模型。

speaker: Unknown
en: We also get Eric's thoughts on why Chain of Thought is getting so weird, including his perspective on the Chain of Thought dialect and the strange language that Astra uses to communicate with sub-agents, plus his pro tips for using Goodfire's Silico research agent, and how he hopes future AI product interfaces will begin to resurface model uncertainty to users.
zh: 我们还听到了 Eric 对思维链为什么变得如此怪异的看法,包括他对「思维链方言」以及 Astra 用来与子智能体交流的奇怪语言的观察,还有他使用 Goodfire 的 Silico 研究智能体的专业技巧,以及他希望未来的 AI 产品界面如何开始把模型的不确定性重新呈现给用户。

speaker: Unknown
en: The bottom line from this conversation and others I've had recently on the future of AI monitoring and control is that chain of thought is increasingly unreliable.
zh: 这场对话,以及我最近其他几场关于 AI 监控与控制未来的对话,得出的底线是:思维链正变得越来越不可靠。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that because these issues seem to correlate not just with RL training, but with the power of the raw pre-trained model itself, this trend might be quite difficult to reverse.
zh: 而且由于这些问题似乎不仅与 RL 训练相关,还与原始预训练模型本身的能力相关,这一趋势可能相当难以逆转。

speaker: Unknown
en: That in turn means that an awful lot, including our ability to understand why agents take the actions they do, may rest on interpretability.
zh: 这反过来意味着,很多很多东西——包括我们理解智能体为何采取其行动的能力——可能都要取决于可解释性。

speaker: Unknown
en: Eric is a pioneer of this research, but as you'll hear, tons of work remains to be done.
zh: Eric 是这一研究的先驱,但正如你将听到的,还有大量工作有待完成。

speaker: Unknown
en: With that, I hope you enjoy this overview of what we know and how much we have left to discover about how AIs decide what to do with Eric Bigelow from GoodFire.
zh: 那么,希望你喜欢这期节目,和来自 Goodfire 的 Eric Bigelow 一起,看看关于 AI 如何决定自己要做什么,我们已经知道什么,以及我们还有多少有待发现。

speaker: Unknown
en: Eric Bigelow, member of technical staff at GoodFire, welcome to the Cognitive Revolution.
zh: Eric Bigelow,Goodfire 的技术成员,欢迎来到 The Cognitive Revolution。

speaker: Unknown
en: Thank you very much, Nathan.
zh: 非常感谢,Nathan。

speaker: Unknown
en: Excited to be here.
zh: 很高兴来到这里。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, I'm excited for this conversation too.
zh: 是啊,我也很期待这次对话。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think this might be the first time in the history, and there's been like 400 episodes of the podcast at this point, that I went to AIs looking for an answer for a very specific question and came back with a name and that name was yours.
zh: 我觉得这可能是节目历史上第一次——这个播客到现在大概已经有 400 期了——我带着一个非常具体的问题去问 AI,然后带着一个名字回来,而那个名字就是你的。

speaker: Unknown
en: So the kind of...
zh: 所以那种……

speaker: Unknown
en: Upstream conversation I had of this one was with Bronson Shane at Apollo, who has the dubious distinction perhaps of having read maybe more chain of thought reasoning than like any other living human, at least any living human who can talk about it all publicly.
zh: 在这次对话之前,我和 Apollo 的 Bronson Shane 聊过,他也许拥有一个不太体面的头衔:读过的思维链推理可能比任何在世的人都多,至少比任何能在公开场合谈论这些的在世人都多。

speaker: Unknown
en: And one of the big takeaways I had from that conversation was he said, you look at these chains of thought.
zh: 我从那次对话中得到的一个重要启示是,他说,你看这些思维链,

speaker: Unknown
en: And the models are thrashing around doing a sort of linearized tree search of possibility.
zh: 模型在里面到处乱撞,做某种线性化的可能性树搜索。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then at some point they make a decision.
zh: 然后在某个时点,它们做出了一个决定。

speaker: Unknown
en: And even having read all the chain of thought that came before that, it's often like very not obvious why they made the decision that they made.
zh: 而即便读完了那之前所有的思维链,往往也很难看出它们为什么做出了那个决定。

speaker: Unknown
en: And you really couldn't have predicted it.
zh: 你真的没法预测到。

speaker: Unknown
en: And in a way that's like kind of human-like, right?
zh: 从某种角度说,这还挺像人类的,对吧?

speaker: Unknown
en: It's how do I make my decisions?
zh: 我是怎么做出我的决定的?

speaker: Unknown
en: I'm not so sure I have great insight into that all the time either.
zh: 我也不太确定我每时每刻对此都有很好的洞察。

speaker: Unknown
en: But this prompted the question, okay, at some point after all this stuff, all this reasoning, all this, again, trying to reason about what the greater wants and all that stuff, eventually we come to a passage and it's like, and so the answer is...
zh: 但这就引出了一个问题:好,在这一切之后,在所有这些推理之后,在所有这些——再说一遍——试图推理更大的意图等等之后,最终我们会看到一段话,它说:「所以答案是……」

speaker: Unknown
en: How does that next token get chosen?
zh: 那下一个 token 是怎么被选中的?

speaker: Unknown
en: That's what I went to the AIs to ask.
zh: 这就是我去问 AI 的问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: Asked for a literature review.
zh: 我让它们做了一次文献综述。

speaker: Unknown
en: And Eric Bigelow came back as the through line through that research.
zh: 而 Eric Bigelow 作为贯穿那项研究的主线浮现了出来。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I was like, I know that company.
zh: 我当时就想,我知道那家公司。

speaker: Unknown
en: I should get to know that guy.
zh: 我应该认识一下那个人。

speaker: Unknown
en: So what I want to do, I think you may know as much or more than any other living human about how these decisions are made.
zh: 所以我想做的是——我觉得关于这些决策是如何做出的,你了解的也许和任何在世的人一样多,甚至更多,

speaker: Unknown
en: And I'm afraid that's maybe not still all that much.
zh: 而且我担心那可能也仍然不算太多。

speaker: Unknown
en: But what I hope to get out of this conversation is a little intellectual history of your work and like,
zh: 但我希望从这次对话中得到的是你工作的些许思想史,以及,

speaker: Unknown
en: The up-to-date understanding of how the hell do these things make decisions?
zh: 对「这些东西到底是怎么做决策的」的最新理解。

speaker: Unknown
en: What do we know about that?
zh: 我们对此知道些什么?

speaker: Unknown
en: And what is our plan to figure out how to understand it better?
zh: 而我们有什么计划来更好地理解它?

speaker: Unknown
en: Because obviously they're making more and more consequential decisions all the time.
zh: 因为显然,它们时时刻刻都在做越来越重大的决策。

speaker: Unknown
en: How does that sound?
zh: 你觉得怎么样?

speaker: Unknown
en: I'm very honored to be the first guest chosen by the AIs.
zh: 我很荣幸成为 AI 们选中的第一位嘉宾。

speaker: Unknown
en: I always, I feel like they, when I talk to Claude, it seems to really get excited about my research, but I'm sure everybody feels that way.
zh: 我总是觉得，当我跟 Claude 交谈时，它似乎真的对我的研究感到兴奋，但我敢肯定每个人都有这种感觉。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think, uh, I think actually talking...
zh: 我认为，呃，我认为实际上谈……

speaker: Unknown
en: Having some conversations around this podcast and some of the things you were asking about makes me think that I actually should devote more effort to this exact question of how decisions are made.
zh: 围绕这期播客的一些对话，以及你问的一些问题，让我觉得我其实应该在这个问题上投入更多精力，也就是决策是如何做出的这个问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I'll give a quick overview of a project that I think is really one of the most informative projects in how I think about how LLMs work at a basic level.
zh: 但我会快速概述一个项目，我认为这个项目真正是塑造我如何在基本层面上思考 LLM 如何工作的最有启发性的项目之一。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that's my project Forking Paths in Neural Text Generation.
zh: 那就是我的项目「神经文本生成中的分叉路径」。

speaker: Unknown
en: And for that, basically, so this was two years ago with, at the time, it was one of the GPT 3.5 models.
zh: 就这个项目而言，基本上，这是两年前做的，当时用的是 GPT 3.5 系列模型之一。

speaker: Unknown
en: And what we do is we take reasoning chains, we give it a chain of, we give it a question and a chain of thought prompt and have it reason through, you know, step by step.
zh: 我们做的是，我们取推理链，我们给它一个问题和一个思维链提示，让它逐步推理。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then every single token in its reasoning, we resample all these completions.
zh: 然后在它推理中的每一个 token 处，我们都重新采样所有这些补全。

speaker: Unknown
en: So we resample like 30 different rollouts at every single token.
zh: 所以我们在每一个 token 处重新采样大约 30 个不同的 rollout。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then from every one of those rollouts, we see what final answer it landed on.
zh: 然后从每一个这样的 rollout 中，我们看它最终落在了什么答案上。

speaker: Unknown
en: And you can aggregate these into various distributions and then do analysis on these distributions.
zh: 你可以把这些聚合成各种分布，然后对这些分布做分析。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I think the most striking part of this is if you arrange it like a multivariate time series, you see these really interesting dynamics that are happening.
zh: 但我认为其中最引人注目的部分是，如果你把它排布成一个多变量时间序列，你会看到一些非常有趣的动态在发生。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I kind of take inspiration from this from some of the learning dynamics work that was coming out around that time, like around grokking and things like this, where there are like these really sharp phase transitions in training and the model just seems to suddenly learn something.
zh: 我从那个时期出现的一些关于学习动态的工作中获得了一些启发，比如关于 grokking 之类的工作，训练中会出现非常剧烈的相变，模型似乎突然学会了某样东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it turns out that you actually have these during reasoning and in context learning as well, where over the course of reasoning,
zh: 事实证明，在推理和上下文学习过程中也确实存在这些现象，在推理的过程中，

speaker: Unknown
en: There will be certain points in reasoning that the model was initially sort of at a 50% chance of this answer and 30% chance of this answer.
zh: 在推理中会有某些点，模型最初大概是 50% 的概率是某个答案、30% 的概率是另一个答案。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then there's some point that it hits where suddenly the distribution changes really dramatically.
zh: 然后会到达某个点，分布突然发生非常剧烈的变化。

speaker: Unknown
en: And often the distribution just kind of collapses onto a final answer as the model sort of.
zh: 而且通常分布就坍缩到某个最终答案上，随着模型某种意义上……

speaker: Unknown
en: You might say decides what it's going to say next.
zh: 你可以说它决定了它接下来要说什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: Although I think I use the word decides here with maybe scare quotes around it, because I think there's some nuance to what that means.
zh: 不过我想我在这里用「决定」这个词可能要加引号，因为我认为这个词的含义有一些细微之处。

speaker: Unknown
en: But one of my big takeaways from this, and I think this also just kind of falls out of thinking about the architecture, but it's nice to have results that really support this too, is that models, even to some extent, when they plan out their responses, what they're actually going to say at every single moment
zh: 但我从中得到的一个重大启示——我认为这其实也能直接从架构的思考中推出来，不过能有结果真正支持这一点也很好——就是模型，甚至在某种程度上当它们规划自己的回应时，它们在每一刻真正要说的话

speaker: Unknown
en: is really determined by like the flip of a coin, which is what token will it generate next.
zh: 其实是由抛硬币决定的，也就是它接下来会生成什么 token。

speaker: Unknown
en: And there is sort of an interface that was really standard and with OpenAI at least at the time, which I think is unfortunately no longer present and I haven't really seen standard interfaces, which is where you could see the log probabilities of all the tokens in a text output you got and you could kind of hover over different tokens and see what are the alternate tokens that could have been generated instead.
zh: 当时有一种非常标准化的接口，至少 OpenAI 那时候有，我认为遗憾的是现在已经没有了，而且我也没有再见到标准化接口里有这个功能，就是你可以看到你得到的文本输出中所有 token 的对数概率，你可以悬停在不同的 token 上，看看原本可以生成哪些替代的 token。

speaker: Unknown
en: And if you do this
zh: 如果你这样做

speaker: Unknown
en: With a lot of text generation, you might realize that you get this one text answer when you ask some question, but really there actually could have been a lot of different answers, and you might ask what would have happened if this word was different from this word.
zh: 用很多文本生成，你可能会意识到你问某个问题时得到了这一个文本答案，但其实本来可能有很多不同的答案，你可能会问，如果这个词不是这个词而是别的词会怎样。

speaker: Unknown
en: And what we found is that there are certain keywords where sometimes the words, if you were to sort of like look at it like a judge,
zh: 我们发现的是，有一些特定的关键词，有时候那些词，如果你像法官一样去看它，

speaker: Unknown
en: You might guess this like the first time that a final answer is mentioned in the reasoning chain, but then there's other times where this distribution changes really dramatically on some sort of arbitrary word, even like a open parenthesis for like, you know, there's one example we have in the paper where it's like kilowatt hours, open parenthesis, KWH.
zh: 你可能会猜是推理链中第一次提到最终答案的地方，但也有其他时候，分布会在某个任意的词上发生非常剧烈的变化，甚至是一个左括号，比如，我们论文里有一个例子，就是「kilowatt hours, 左括号, KWH」。

speaker: Unknown
en: And, you know, you never expect that to really change how the final answer plays out.
zh: 而且，你知道，你绝不会预期那会真正改变最终答案的走向。

speaker: Unknown
en: But if you actually go to that exact token with this model and you just resample a bunch of text generations, you see that in cases where it's not an open parenthesis, where it starts to be some other just arbitrary word, it ends up being a different final answer.
zh: 但如果你真的用这个模型跳到那个确切的 token，重新采样一大堆文本生成，你会发现，在不是左括号的情况下，是某个别的任意词的情况下，它最终会是一个不同的最终答案。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, um, I think
zh: 所以，呃，我认为

speaker: Unknown
en: This thinking about decisions in LLMs or what they're going to say next very much being determined by sort of chance and by whatever tokens are sampled is really I think the foundation for how I think about a lot of things in LLMs.
zh: 这种认为 LLM 中的决策、即它接下来会说什么，很大程度上是由概率和采样到什么 token 所决定的思考方式，真的是我思考 LLM 中很多事情的基础。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think it sort of shapes how I think about like beliefs and models and sort of what's considered like a factor of hallucination can be dependent on what tokens were generated before it.
zh: 我认为它在某种程度上塑造了我如何思考信念和模型，以及什么被视为幻觉的因素，可能取决于在它之前生成了什么 token。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think one of the properties of reasoning that really comes into play here is self-consistency.
zh: 我认为在这里真正起作用的推理的一个特性是自洽性。

speaker: Unknown
en: So if there's a long reasoning chain that is self-consistent and it sort of generates some token earlier in the chain of suppose that this was the year instead of this was the year.
zh: 所以如果有一条长的推理链是自洽的，而它在链的较早位置生成了某个 token，比如假设「这是这一年」而不是「这是这一年」。

speaker: Unknown
en: If it thinks that the year is 2024 instead of 2026, actually the answer to a question might be very different.
zh: 如果它认为那一年是 2024 而不是 2026，实际上某个问题的答案可能就会非常不同。

speaker: Unknown
en: And there's cases like this where it's like you might think, well, obviously there's like a ground truth.
zh: 也有像这样的情况，你可能会想，嗯，显然是有一个真值的。

speaker: Unknown
en: If I'm asking who is the current head of state, there is a current year, which right now is 2026.
zh: 如果我问谁是现任国家元首，是有一个当前年份的，而现在就是 2026。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so the model was hallucinating.
zh: 所以模型是在产生幻觉。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I think there's also a lot of use cases with LLMs where we don't really know what the ground truth are.
zh: 但我认为也有很多使用 LLM 的场景，我们其实并不知道真值是什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: And there's sort of this branching space of possibilities that we actually want to explore naturally when we're interacting with a model.
zh: 而且存在某种分支的可能性空间，我们在与模型交互时其实想要自然地去探索它。
